claim: The crystal structure of Munc13-1 C1C2BMUN reveals a 19.5 nm-long multi-helical structure with the C1 and C2B domains packed at one end.
source: The crystal structure of a Munc13–1 fragment including its C1, C2B and MUN domains (C1C2BMUN) reveals a 19.5 nm-long multi-helical structure with the C1 and C2B domains packed at one end.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by crystallographic data presented in the manuscript, including structural coordinates and measurements.

claim: The similar orientations of the diacylglycerol- and Ca2+-binding sites of the C1 and C2B domains suggest that the two domains cooperate in plasma-membrane binding.
source: The similar orientations of the respective diacyglycerol- and Ca2+-binding sites of the C1 and C2B domains suggest that the two domains cooperate in plasma-membrane binding and that activation of Munc13–1 by Ca2+ and diacylglycerol during short-term presynaptic plasticity are closely interrelated.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the structural arrangement observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Activation of Munc13-1 by Ca2+ and diacylglycerol during short-term presynaptic plasticity are closely interrelated.
source: The similar orientations of the respective diacyglycerol- and Ca2+-binding sites of the C1 and C2B domains suggest that the two domains cooperate in plasma-membrane binding and that activation of Munc13–1 by Ca2+ and diacylglycerol during short-term presynaptic plasticity are closely interrelated.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural proximity of the binding sites in the crystal structure.

claim: The C1C2BMUN structure imposes key constraints for models of neurotransmitter release.
source: The structure imposes key constraints for models of neurotransmitter release and suggests that Munc13–1 bridges the vesicle and plasma membranes from the periphery of the membrane-membrane interface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural dimensions and domain arrangements observed.

claim: Munc13-1 bridges the vesicle and plasma membranes from the periphery of the membrane-membrane interface.
source: The structure imposes key constraints for models of neurotransmitter release and suggests that Munc13–1 bridges the vesicle and plasma membranes from the periphery of the membrane-membrane interface.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the elongated structure and domain arrangement.

claim: Neurotransmitter release by synaptic vesicle exocytosis is critical for neuronal communication.
source: The release of neurotransmitters by synaptic vesicle exocytosis is critical for neuronal communication.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge in the field of neuroscience.

claim: Neurotransmitter release involves tethering of synaptic vesicles to active zones, priming, and Ca2+-triggered membrane fusion.
source: This exquisitely regulated process involves several steps, including tethering of synaptic vesicles to specialized sites of the presynaptic plasma membrane called active zones, a priming step(s) that leaves the vesicles ready to release, and Ca2+-triggered membrane fusion (Südhof, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Each step of neurotransmitter release can be modulated in presynaptic plasticity processes that underlie multiple forms of information processing in the brain.
source: Each of these steps can be modulated in a variety of presynaptic plasticity processes that underlie multiple forms of information processing in the brain (Regehr, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established literature.

claim: Neuronal SNAREs synaptobrevin, syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25 play a key role in membrane fusion by forming a tight four-helix bundle.
source: The protein machinery that controls release (Rizo and Xu, 2015; Jahn and Fasshauer, 2012; Südhof and Rothman, 2009) includes the neuronal soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptors (SNAREs) synaptobrevin, syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25, which play a key role in membrane fusion by forming a tight four-helix bundle (the SNARE complex) that brings the vesicle and plasma membranes into close proximity (Söllner et al., 1993; Hanson et al., 1997; Poirier et al., 1998; Sutton et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established structural and functional studies.

claim: The SNARE complex brings the vesicle and plasma membranes into close proximity.
source: The protein machinery that controls release (Rizo and Xu, 2015; Jahn and Fasshauer, 2012; Südhof and Rothman, 2009) includes the neuronal soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptors (SNAREs) synaptobrevin, syntaxin-1 and SNAP-25, which play a key role in membrane fusion by forming a tight four-helix bundle (the SNARE complex) that brings the vesicle and plasma membranes into close proximity (Söllner et al., 1993; Hanson et al., 1997; Poirier et al., 1998; Sutton et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established structural and functional studies.

claim: The SNARE complex is disassembled by NSF and SNAPs to recycle the SNAREs for another round of fusion.
source: This complex is disassembled by N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor (NSF) and soluble NSF attachment proteins (SNAPs; no relation to SNAP-25) (Söllner et al., 1993) to recycle the SNAREs for another round of fusion (Mayer et al., 1996; Banerjee et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Munc18-1 and Munc13s are crucial for neurotransmitter release.
source: The Sec1/Munc18 protein Munc18–1 and the large (200 kDa) active zone proteins called Munc13s are also crucial for release.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the literature cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Munc18-1 binds to a self-inhibited 'closed' conformation of syntaxin-1.
source: Munc18–1 binds to a self-inhibited 'closed' conformation of syntaxin-1 (Dulubova et al., 1999; Misura et al., 2000) and orchestrates SNARE complex assembly in an NSF-SNAP-resistant manner together with Munc13, which helps to open syntaxin-1 (Richmond et al., 2001; Ma et al., 2011, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Munc18-1 orchestrates SNARE complex assembly in an NSF-SNAP-resistant manner together with Munc13.
source: Munc18–1 binds to a self-inhibited 'closed' conformation of syntaxin-1 (Dulubova et al., 1999; Misura et al., 2000) and orchestrates SNARE complex assembly in an NSF-SNAP-resistant manner together with Munc13, which helps to open syntaxin-1 (Richmond et al., 2001; Ma et al., 2011, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Munc13 helps to open syntaxin-1.
source: Munc18–1 binds to a self-inhibited 'closed' conformation of syntaxin-1 (Dulubova et al., 1999; Misura et al., 2000) and orchestrates SNARE complex assembly in an NSF-SNAP-resistant manner together with Munc13, which helps to open syntaxin-1 (Richmond et al., 2001; Ma et al., 2011, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Neurotransmitter release is completely abrogated in the absence of Munc13s.
source: Thus, neurotransmitter release is completely abrogated in the absence of Munc13s (Augustin et al., 1999; Richmond et al., 1999; Aravamudan et al., 1999; Varoqueaux et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic knockout studies.

claim: Munc13s play key roles in docking and priming.
source: This phenotype most likely arises because Munc13s play key roles in docking and priming (Varoqueaux et al., 2002; Weimer et al., 2006; Hammarlund et al., 2007; Imig et al., 2014) that are associated at least in part to their activity in opening syntaxin-1 and thus stimulating SNARE complex formation through their MUN domain (Richmond et al., 2001; Basu et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: The docking and priming activity of Munc13s is associated at least in part to their activity in opening syntaxin-1 and stimulating SNARE complex formation through their MUN domain.
source: This phenotype most likely arises because Munc13s play key roles in docking and priming (Varoqueaux et al., 2002; Weimer et al., 2006; Hammarlund et al., 2007; Imig et al., 2014) that are associated at least in part to their activity in opening syntaxin-1 and thus stimulating SNARE complex formation through their MUN domain (Richmond et al., 2001; Basu et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional and structural studies.

claim: The C1-C2B region and the C-terminal C2C domain are critical for neurotransmitter release.
source: However, the C1-C2B region and the C-terminal C2C domain are also critical for release, which may arise because these domains help bridge the vesicle and plasma membranes (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a functional study.

claim: The C1-C2B region and C2C domain may help bridge the vesicle and plasma membranes.
source: However, the C1-C2B region and the C-terminal C2C domain are also critical for release, which may arise because these domains help bridge the vesicle and plasma membranes (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of functional data supported by citation.

claim: There is evidence for a role of Munc13s in events downstream of priming.
source: There is also evidence for a role of Munc13s in events downstream of priming [e.g. (Hammarlund et al., 2007; Shin et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Munc13s are involved in multiple presynaptic plasticity processes, including isoform-specific depression and augmentation.
source: Moreover, Munc13s are involved in multiple presynaptic plasticity processes, including isoform-specific depression and augmentation (Rosenmund et al., 2002), diacyglycerol (DAG)-phorbol ester-dependent potentiation of release via the C1 domain (Rhee et al., 2002) and Ca2+-dependent short-term plasticity through the C2B domain and a calmodulin-binding region (Shin et al., 2010; Junge et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Munc13s mediate DAG-phorbol ester-dependent potentiation of release via the C1 domain.
source: Moreover, Munc13s are involved in multiple presynaptic plasticity processes, including isoform-specific depression and augmentation (Rosenmund et al., 2002), diacyglycerol (DAG)-phorbol ester-dependent potentiation of release via the C1 domain (Rhee et al., 2002) and Ca2+-dependent short-term plasticity through the C2B domain and a calmodulin-binding region (Shin et al., 2010; Junge et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a functional study.

claim: Munc13s mediate Ca2+-dependent short-term plasticity through the C2B domain and a calmodulin-binding region.
source: Moreover, Munc13s are involved in multiple presynaptic plasticity processes, including isoform-specific depression and augmentation (Rosenmund et al., 2002), diacyglycerol (DAG)-phorbol ester-dependent potentiation of release via the C1 domain (Rhee et al., 2002) and Ca2+-dependent short-term plasticity through the C2B domain and a calmodulin-binding region (Shin et al., 2010; Junge et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Binding of the Munc13-1 C2A domain to RIMs provides a connection to RIM-dependent forms of short- and long-term presynaptic plasticity.
source: Binding of the Munc13–1 C2A domain to RIMs also provides a connection to RIM-dependent forms of short- and long-term presynaptic plasticity (Betz et al., 2001; Dulubova et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: Knock-in mice bearing a point mutation in the Munc13-1 C1 domain that disrupts phorbol-ester-dependent potentiation of release die 2-3 hr after birth.
source: The crucial physiological importance of these modulatory processes was emphatically illustrated by the finding that knock-in mice bearing a point mutation in the Munc13–1 C1 domain that disrupts phorbol-ester-dependent potentiation of release die 2–3 hr after birth even though the mutation causes no impairment of evoked release (Rhee et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a genetic study.

claim: The C1 domain mutation that disrupts phorbol-ester-dependent potentiation causes no impairment of evoked release.
source: The crucial physiological importance of these modulatory processes was emphatically illustrated by the finding that knock-in mice bearing a point mutation in the Munc13–1 C1 domain that disrupts phorbol-ester-dependent potentiation of release die 2–3 hr after birth even though the mutation causes no impairment of evoked release (Rhee et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a genetic study.

claim: The structure of C1C2BMUN contains 26 α-helices.
source: The structure of C1C2BMUN can be viewed as a highly elongated rod spanning ca. 195 Å and is formed mostly of α-helical bundles, with a total of 26 helices; the C1 and C2B domains pack at the N-terminal end of the rod (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure data.

claim: The MUN domain is homologous to subunits of complexes that mediate tethering in diverse membrane compartments.
source: Much of the long rod is formed by the MUN domain, which is homologous to subunits of complexes that mediate tethering in diverse membrane compartments (Pei et al., 2009; Yu and Hughson, 2010) and was previously shown to be formed by four subdomains of about five helices each (named A-D and colored in blue, green, yellow and orange on Figure 1) (Li et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to comparative structural studies.

claim: The MUN domain was previously shown to be formed by four subdomains of about five helices each.
source: Much of the long rod is formed by the MUN domain, which is homologous to subunits of complexes that mediate tethering in diverse membrane compartments (Pei et al., 2009; Yu and Hughson, 2010) and was previously shown to be formed by four subdomains of about five helices each (named A-D and colored in blue, green, yellow and orange on Figure 1) (Li et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The MUN domain in C1C2BMUN actually starts at residue 828 and contains five additional helices (helices H6-H10), resulting in a total of seven helices for subdomain A.
source: However, the structure of C1C2BMUN shows that the MUN domain actually starts at residue 828 and contains five additional helices (helices H6-H10), resulting in a total of seven helices for subdomain A (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a new finding from the crystal structure data presented in this study.

claim: There are five helices preceding the MUN domain (helices H1-H5).
source: In addition, there are five more helices preceding the MUN domain (helices H1-H5; Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure data.

claim: Four of the helices preceding the MUN domain correspond to the linker sequence between the C1 and C2B domains.
source: Four of these helices correspond to the linker sequence between the C1 and C2B domains, whereas one helix (H1) is spanned by a sequence preceding the C1 domain (colored in red).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure data.

claim: There are extensive contacts between helix H1, the four helices of the linker, the MUN domain, the C1 domain and the C2B domain.
source: As the structure of C1C2BMUN now reveals, there are extensive contacts between helix H1, the four helices of the linker, the MUN domain, the C1 domain and the C2B domain (Figure 1B,D–F), and hence it is not surprising that elimination of some of these interfaces impairs proper folding.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure data.

claim: The structures of the C1 and C2B domains in C1C2BMUN are similar to those determined for the isolated domains.
source: We also note that the structures of the C1 and C2B domains in C1C2BMUN are similar to those determined for the isolated domains (Shen et al., 2005; Shin et al., 2010), although the Ca2+-binding loops are not visible in the C2B domain of C1C2BMUN (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on comparison of crystal structures.

claim: The Ca2+-binding loops are not visible in the C2B domain of C1C2BMUN.
source: We also note that the structures of the C1 and C2B domains in C1C2BMUN are similar to those determined for the isolated domains (Shen et al., 2005; Shin et al., 2010), although the Ca2+-binding loops are not visible in the C2B domain of C1C2BMUN (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure data.

claim: The Ca2+-binding loops were observable in the crystal structure of the C2B domain bound to Ca2+ but not in its crystal structure without Ca2+.
source: This correlates with the previous finding that these loops were observable in the crystal structure of the C2B domain bound to Ca2+ but not in its crystal structure without Ca2+ (Shin et al., 2010), as our C1C2BMUN structure was determined in the absence of Ca2+.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous structural study.

claim: The C1C2BMUN structure was determined in the absence of Ca2+.
source: This correlates with the previous finding that these loops were observable in the crystal structure of the C2B domain bound to Ca2+ but not in its crystal structure without Ca2+ (Shin et al., 2010), as our C1C2BMUN structure was determined in the absence of Ca2+.
evidence: This is a methodological detail of the crystallographic experiment.

claim: The elongated structure and overall packing of the different domains at the N-terminal end suggest that C1C2BMUN may function as a rigid or semi-rigid unit that bridges the synaptic vesicle and plasma membranes.
source: First, the elongated structure and the overall packing of the different domains at the N-terminal end of the structure suggest that C1C2BMUN may function as a rigid or semi-rigid unit that bridges the synaptic vesicle and plasma membranes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural features observed.

claim: The similarity in the structures of the two molecules from the asymmetric unit of the C1C2BMUN crystals suggests that the overall architecture of C1C2BMUN has limited flexibility.
source: Note in this context that the similarity in the structures of the two molecules from the asymmetric unit of the C1C2BMUN crystals (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and between these structures and that of the nearly complete MUN domain (Figure 1C) suggest that the overall architecture of C1C2BMUN has limited flexibility.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of crystal structures.

claim: The Ca2+-binding loops of the C2B domain mediate its interactions with PIP2-containing membranes in a Ca2+-dependent manner.
source: Second, a model of the structure of C1C2BMUN incorporating the Ca2+-binding loops of the C2B domain, which mediate its interactions with PIP2-containing membranes in a Ca2+-dependent manner (Shin et al., 2010), shows that these loops are proximal to the DAG-phorbol ester-binding region of the C1 domain (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous functional study.

claim: The Ca2+-binding loops of the C2B domain are proximal to the DAG-phorbol ester-binding region of the C1 domain.
source: Second, a model of the structure of C1C2BMUN incorporating the Ca2+-binding loops of the C2B domain, which mediate its interactions with PIP2-containing membranes in a Ca2+-dependent manner (Shin et al., 2010), shows that these loops are proximal to the DAG-phorbol ester-binding region of the C1 domain (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling using the crystal structure data.

claim: The arrangement of C1 and C2B domains is expected to promote cooperation between the two domains in membrane binding.
source: This arrangement is expected to promote cooperation between the C1 and C2B domains in membrane binding, thus suggesting a natural mechanism for synergy between increases in DAG and intracellular Ca2+ concentrations to enhance release probability upon repetitive stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural arrangement.

claim: The arrangement of C1 and C2B domains suggests a natural mechanism for synergy between increases in DAG and intracellular Ca2+ concentrations to enhance release probability upon repetitive stimulation.
source: This arrangement is expected to promote cooperation between the C1 and C2B domains in membrane binding, thus suggesting a natural mechanism for synergy between increases in DAG and intracellular Ca2+ concentrations to enhance release probability upon repetitive stimulation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural data.

claim: There are abundant basic residues in the C1-C2B region that could potentially mediate membrane binding in alternative orientations in the absence of DAG and Ca2+-bound to the C2B domain.
source: However, it is noteworthy that there are abundant basic residues in the C1-C2B region (Figure 2A) that could potentially mediate membrane binding in alternative orientations in the absence of DAG and Ca2+-bound to the C2B domain (e.g. Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure and a speculation about function.

claim: Increased DAG and intracellular Ca2+ concentrations may alter release probability by promoting a different orientation of the Munc13-1 C-terminal region that is more efficient in promoting priming and/or fusion.
source: These observations suggest that increased DAG and intracellular Ca2+ concentrations may alter release probability by promoting a different orientation of the Munc13–1 C-terminal region that is more efficient in promoting priming and/or fusion (see Discussion and models described therein).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural observations.

claim: Helix H1 is packed against the MUN domain, with the N-terminus pointing toward the center of the long rod.
source: Third, the finding that helix H1 is packed against the MUN domain, with the N-terminus pointing toward the center of the long rod (Figure 1B), suggests that N-terminal sequences of Munc13–1 not included in this structure could perform their regulatory functions by influencing MUN domain activity.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure data.

claim: N-terminal sequences of Munc13-1 not included in the C1C2BMUN structure could perform their regulatory functions by influencing MUN domain activity.
source: Third, the finding that helix H1 is packed against the MUN domain, with the N-terminus pointing toward the center of the long rod (Figure 1B), suggests that N-terminal sequences of Munc13–1 not included in this structure could perform their regulatory functions by influencing MUN domain activity.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the structural arrangement.

claim: The calmodulin-binding region of Munc13-1 might inhibit release by binding to the middle of the MUN domain where an NF sequence is critical for opening syntaxin-1.
source: For instance, the calmodulin-binding region of Munc13–1 might inhibit release by binding to the middle of the MUN domain, where an NF sequence (Figure 1B) is known to be critical for opening syntaxin-1 (Yang et al., 2015), and binding of Ca2+-calmodulin to this region may enhance release by relieving this inhibition.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the structure and cited functional data.

claim: Binding of Ca2+-calmodulin to the calmodulin-binding region may enhance release by relieving inhibition.
source: For instance, the calmodulin-binding region of Munc13–1 might inhibit release by binding to the middle of the MUN domain, where an NF sequence (Figure 1B) is known to be critical for opening syntaxin-1 (Yang et al., 2015), and binding of Ca2+-calmodulin to this region may enhance release by relieving this inhibition.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the structure.

claim: An NF sequence in the MUN domain is critical for opening syntaxin-1.
source: For instance, the calmodulin-binding region of Munc13–1 might inhibit release by binding to the middle of the MUN domain, where an NF sequence (Figure 1B) is known to be critical for opening syntaxin-1 (Yang et al., 2015), and binding of Ca2+-calmodulin to this region may enhance release by relieving this inhibition.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous functional study.

claim: Interactions of homodimerized Munc13-1 C2A domain with the MUN domain might underlie the inhibition caused by homodimerization, which is relieved by RIM binding.
source: Interactions of homodimerized Munc13–1 C2A domain (Lu et al., 2006) with the MUN domain might also underlie the inhibition caused by homodimerization, which is relieved by RIM binding (Deng et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the structure and cited functional data.

claim: The V549E,L554E mutation increases mEPSC frequency.
source: Only the V549E,L554E mutation in the N-terminal H1 helix showed an increase in mEPSC frequency, whereas the mEPSC charge and amplitude were unchanged (Figure 3).
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The V549E,L554E mutation does not change mEPSC charge and amplitude.
source: Only the V549E,L554E mutation in the N-terminal H1 helix showed an increase in mEPSC frequency, whereas the mEPSC charge and amplitude were unchanged (Figure 3).
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The R750E,K752E mutation impairs Ca2+-triggered release.
source: Analysis of the EPSC amplitudes revealed that the R750E,K752E mutation in the C1-C2B interface and the N940W mutation in the C2B-MUN interface impaired Ca2+-triggered release (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The N940W mutation impairs Ca2+-triggered release.
source: Analysis of the EPSC amplitudes revealed that the R750E,K752E mutation in the C1-C2B interface and the N940W mutation in the C2B-MUN interface impaired Ca2+-triggered release (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments.

claim: Expression of the V549E,L554E mutant fully rescued evoked release.
source: However, expression of the V549E,L554E mutant where helix H1 is perturbed fully rescued evoked release.
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The N940W mutation causes a decrease in RRP size of close to 40%.
source: We found that the N940W mutation in the C2B-MUN interface caused a decrease in RRP size of close to 40%, similar to the change seen in the evoked response.
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments using sucrose application.

claim: The V549E,L554E mutation decreased the RRP size by nearly 50%.
source: The H1 helix mutation V549E,L554E decreased the RRP size by nearly 50% (Figure 4C,D), which contrasts with the lack of an effect of this mutation on evoked release.
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments using sucrose application.

claim: The R750E,K752E mutation led to normal vesicle priming despite reducing the evoked response.
source: Furthermore, the disruption of the C1-C2B interface by the R750E,K752E mutation led to normal vesicle priming despite reducing the evoked response.
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The three mutations differentially regulate the efficiency of the vesicle fusion process.
source: These experiments demonstrate that all three mutations impact Munc13–1 function but, interestingly, each mutation displays distinct effects on evoked release and vesicle priming. This finding strongly suggests that the domain interfaces differentially regulate the efficiency of the vesicle fusion process, which may lead to differences in vesicle release probability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects observed in electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The V549E,L554E mutation increased the vesicular release probability significantly.
source: The V549E,L554E mutation in the H1 helix increased the vesicular release probability significantly, as expected, while the small differences in Pvr observed for the R750E,K752E and N940W mutants with respect to WT were not statistically significant (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is calculated from electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The small differences in Pvr observed for the R750E,K752E and N940W mutants with respect to WT were not statistically significant.
source: The V549E,L554E mutation in the H1 helix increased the vesicular release probability significantly, as expected, while the small differences in Pvr observed for the R750E,K752E and N940W mutants with respect to WT were not statistically significant (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: The V549E,L554E mutant showed more depression in paired-pulse experiments compared to WT.
source: Compared to WT, the V549E,L554E mutant showed more depression, in correlation with our finding of enhanced release probability, while the other two mutants showed similar paired-pulse behavior to WT rescues, in agreement with the conclusion that these mutations did not disrupt basal release probability substantially.
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The R750E,K752E and N940W mutants showed similar paired-pulse behavior to WT rescues.
source: Compared to WT, the V549E,L554E mutant showed more depression, in correlation with our finding of enhanced release probability, while the other two mutants showed similar paired-pulse behavior to WT rescues, in agreement with the conclusion that these mutations did not disrupt basal release probability substantially.
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The V549E,L554E mutation caused more pronounced depression of sustained release than expected from the initial release probability.
source: Interestingly, the V549E,L554E mutation in the H1 helix and the R750E,K752E mutation in the C1-C2B interface caused more pronounced depression of sustained release than expected from the initial release probability, while disrupting the C2B-MUN interface with the N940W mutation caused less depression than expected from the initial release probability (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments during 10 Hz stimulation.

claim: The R750E,K752E mutation caused more pronounced depression of sustained release than expected from the initial release probability.
source: Interestingly, the V549E,L554E mutation in the H1 helix and the R750E,K752E mutation in the C1-C2B interface caused more pronounced depression of sustained release than expected from the initial release probability, while disrupting the C2B-MUN interface with the N940W mutation caused less depression than expected from the initial release probability (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments during 10 Hz stimulation.

claim: The N940W mutation caused less depression than expected from the initial release probability.
source: Interestingly, the V549E,L554E mutation in the H1 helix and the R750E,K752E mutation in the C1-C2B interface caused more pronounced depression of sustained release than expected from the initial release probability, while disrupting the C2B-MUN interface with the N940W mutation caused less depression than expected from the initial release probability (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments during 10 Hz stimulation.

claim: Each one of the interfaces disrupted by the mutations plays a role in activity-dependent vesicle re-priming.
source: These results suggest that each one of the interfaces disrupted by the mutations plays a role in activity-dependent vesicle re-priming, and reinforce the notion that Munc13 exerts multiple functions in shaping release properties at synapses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects observed during repetitive stimulation.

claim: The N940W mutation showed more pronounced potentiation by PDBu than WT Munc13-1.
source: The N940W mutation in the C2B-MUN interface showed more pronounced potentiation than WT Munc13–1 (Figure 6B), which correlates with the reduction in steady-state depression during 10 Hz AP trains observed for this mutant (Figure 5C) and indicates an easier transition for Munc13–1 to a potentiated state.
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments with PDBu application.

claim: The V549E,L554E mutation led to reduced potentiation by PDBu compared to WT.
source: Conversely, the V549E,L554E in helix H1 led to reduced potentiation by PDBu compared to WT, which likely arises because of the initial high vesicular release probability observed for this mutant (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments with PDBu application.

claim: The R750E,K752E mutation caused an even more pronounced decrease in PDBu potentiation.
source: Remarkably, the R750E,K752E mutation in the C1-C2B interface caused an even more pronounced decrease in PDBu potentiation (Figure 6B), which contrasts with the limited effect of this mutation on vesicular release probability (Figure 4E) but correlates with the strong depression observed in the 10 Hz AP trains (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments with PDBu application.

claim: The interactions between the C1 and C2B domain observed in the crystal structure are critical for the interplay between the two domains in Ca2+- and DAG-dependent presynaptic plasticity.
source: These findings strongly support the notion that the interactions between the C1 and C2B domain observed in our crystal structure are critical for the interplay between the two domains in Ca2+- and DAG-dependent presynaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined structural and functional data.

claim: For WT Munc13-1 rescues, the RRP size after a 10 Hz train tended to decrease compared to the RRP size before the train, but the difference was not significant.
source: For rescues with WT Munc13–1 and the three mutants, the RRP size after the train tended to decrease compared to the RRP size before the train, but the difference was not significant (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The EPSC amplitude increased for the WT rescue after a 10 Hz train.
source: On the other hand, the EPSC amplitude increased for the WT rescue after the train (Figure 7D,F), thus leading to an increased release probability with respect to the Pvr observed before the train (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments.

claim: In WT rescues, a 10 Hz train does not have a substantial effect on the RRP, but the efficiency of evoked release increases.
source: These results indicate that in the WT rescues the train does not have a substantial effect on the RRP, but the efficiency of evoked release increases due to some alteration(s) of the release machinery.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The V549E,L554E mutation showed a failure to potentiate the RRP size and a failure to increase the vesicular release probability after a 10 Hz train.
source: In rescues with the V549E,L554E mutation in helix H1, comparison of RRP size and release probability before and after a 10 Hz train showed a failure to potentiate the RRP size, as observed in the WT rescue, but also a failure to increase the vesicular release probability (Figure 7B,E).
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The enhanced depression during the AP train observed for the V549E,L554E mutant was due to a failure to potentiate release probability and not due to a failure in vesicle replenishment.
source: Thus, the enhanced depression during the AP train observed for this mutant compared to WT Munc13–1 (Figure 5C) was due to a failure to potentiate release probability and not due to a failure in vesicle replenishment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The R750E,K752E mutation showed no impairment of RRP size and vesicular release probability in naïve synapses, but enhanced depression of EPSC responses during AP trains.
source: Similar results were obtained for the rescue with Munc13–1 bearing the R750E,K752E mutation in the C1-C2B interface (Figure 7B,D–F), which in naïve synapses caused no impairment of RRP size and vesicular release probability (Figure 4D,E), but an enhanced depression of EPSC responses during AP trains (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The enhanced depression for the R750E,K752E mutant was not due to a failure in vesicle replenishment but to a failure to potentiate release probability.
source: Thus, this enhanced depression was not due to a failure in vesicle replenishment but to a failure to potentiate release probability, as observed for the V549E,L554E mutant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The N940W mutation caused a selective increase in vesicular release probability after a 10 Hz AP train, similar to what is seen in WT rescues but with larger degree of potentiation.
source: Finally, the N940W mutation in the C2B-MUN interface, which leads to a 40% reduction in RRP size (Figure 4D) but no change in release probability (Figure 4E) in naive synapses, caused a selective increase in vesicular release probability after the AP train, similar to what is seen in WT rescues but with larger degree of potentiation (Figure 7B,D–F).
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The N940W mutant exhibits much less depression than WT during a 10 Hz train because this mutant is more likely to potentiate release probability during AP trains than WT Munc13-1.
source: Thus, the finding that this mutant exhibits much less depression than WT during the AP train (Figure 5C) arises because this mutant is more likely to potentiate release probability during AP trains than WT Munc13–1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The electrophysiological data provide compelling evidence for functional and structural interactions among the domains of the Munc13-1 C1C2BMUN fragment.
source: Overall, our electrophysiological data provide compelling evidence for functional and structural interactions among the domains of the Munc13–1 C1C2BMUN fragment.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the electrophysiological data presented.

claim: The domain interactions play distinct roles in regulating vesicle priming, vesicle release probability and activity-dependent changes in release probability.
source: These interactions play distinct roles in regulating vesicle priming, vesicle release probability and activity-dependent changes in release probability, thus having different impact on the ability of synapses to dynamically respond to incoming AP patterns.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the electrophysiological data presented.

claim: Reconstitution experiments with C1C2BMUNC2C recapitulate multiple features of neurotransmitter release, including the absolute requirement of Munc18-1 and Munc13-1 for membrane fusion.
source: Our reconstitution experiments, which monitor fusion between synaptobrevin liposomes (V-liposomes) and syntaxin-1-SNAP-25 liposomes (T-liposomes) in the presence of Munc18–1, NSF, αSNAP and a Munc13–1 fragment spanning its C1, C2B, MUN and C2C domains (C1C2BMUNC2C), recapitulate multiple features of neurotransmitter release, in particular the absolute requirement of Munc18–1 and Munc13–1 for membrane fusion (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous reconstitution study.

claim: Multiple attempts to express C1C2BMUNC2C bearing the V549E,L554E mutation failed to yield sufficient amounts of soluble protein.
source: Unfortunately, multiple attempts to express C1C2BMUNC2C bearing the V549E,L554E mutation failed to yield sufficient amounts of soluble protein, and we were also unable to obtain C1C2BMUNC2C bearing a single V549E or L554E mutation, suggesting that both substitutions strongly destabilize the fragment.
evidence: This is a direct observation from protein expression experiments.

claim: The V549E,L554E mutation strongly destabilizes the C1C2BMUNC2C fragment.
source: Unfortunately, multiple attempts to express C1C2BMUNC2C bearing the V549E,L554E mutation failed to yield sufficient amounts of soluble protein, and we were also unable to obtain C1C2BMUNC2C bearing a single V549E or L554E mutation, suggesting that both substitutions strongly destabilize the fragment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the protein expression results.

claim: The V549E,L554E mutation may be less destabilizing in neurons because of interactions with N-terminal sequences of Munc13-1, with other components of the release machinery, or with molecular chaperones.
source: Since the V549E,L554E mutant was expressed at levels comparable to WT Munc13–1 in our rescue experiments, it is plausible that this mutation is less destabilizing in the context of these experiments because of interactions of that region with N-terminal sequences of Munc13–1, with other components of the release machinery, or with molecular chaperones.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the difference between in vitro and in vivo expression.

claim: Under standard reconstitution conditions with 500 nM C1C2BMUNC2C and T-liposomes containing DAG and PIP2, fusion is highly efficient upon Ca2+ addition.
source: Under the standard conditions of our experiments, in which we use 500 nM C1C2BMUNC2C and we include DAG and PIP2 in the T-liposomes, fusion is highly efficient upon Ca2+ addition and the Ca2+ dependence arises from Ca2+ binding to the C2B domain (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous reconstitution study.

claim: The Ca2+ dependence of fusion in reconstitution experiments arises from Ca2+ binding to the C2B domain.
source: Under the standard conditions of our experiments, in which we use 500 nM C1C2BMUNC2C and we include DAG and PIP2 in the T-liposomes, fusion is highly efficient upon Ca2+ addition and the Ca2+ dependence arises from Ca2+ binding to the C2B domain (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous reconstitution study.

claim: When T-liposomes contained DAG and PIP2, the N940W mutation slightly impaired fusion while the R750E,K752E mutation led to a considerably stronger impairment.
source: When the T-liposomes contained DAG and PIP2, the N940W mutation in the C2B-MUN interface slightly impaired fusion while the R750E,K752E mutation in the C1-C2B interface led to a considerably stronger impairment (Figure 8A,B; see Figure 8—figure supplement 2 for quantification).
evidence: This is directly measured in reconstitution experiments.

claim: The impairment of fusion by the R750E,K752E mutation became more overt with T-liposomes containing only DAG or only PIP2.
source: This impairment became more overt with T-liposomes containing only DAG or only PIP2, while the effects of the N940W mutation remained mild (Figure 8C–F).
evidence: This is directly measured in reconstitution experiments.

claim: A 'reversal' quadruple mutant (R750E,K752E,E582R,E584K) partially compensated for the effects of the R750E,K752E mutation.
source: To test whether the effects of the R750E,K752E mutation in these experiments are indeed due to disruption of the C1-C2B interface, we made a 'reversal' quadruple mutant where we mutated two of the acidic residues from the C1 domain in its interface with the C2B domain (Figure 1E) to basic residues (R750E,K752E,E582R,E584K). These two additional substitutions partially compensated for the effects of the R750E,K752E mutation, as the quadruple mutation recovered some of the activity lost in the R750E,K752E mutant (Figure 8).
evidence: This is directly measured in reconstitution experiments.

claim: The functional recovery in the quadruple mutant supports the notion that the effects of the R750E,K752E mutation in the fusion assays are due to disruption of C1-C2B interactions.
source: Hence, the observed functional recovery in the quadruple mutant supports the notion that the effects of the R750E,K752E mutation in the fusion assays are due to disruption of C1-C2B interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reconstitution data with the reversal mutant.

claim: The impairment of fusion caused by the R750E,K752E mutation in reconstitution assays correlates with the impairment of evoked release observed in rescue experiments.
source: The impairment of fusion caused by the R750E,K752E in our reconstitution assays correlates with the impairment of evoked release observed in the rescue experiments, as well as with the strong depression observed for this mutation in the 10 Hz trains and the impairment of PDBu-induced augmentation (Figures 4–6).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: The results strongly support that the C1-C2B interface observed in the crystal structure is important for evoked release and for cooperation between the C1 and C2B domains in membrane binding during repetitive stimulation.
source: Altogether, our results strongly support the notion that the C1-C2B interface observed in the crystal structure of C1C2BMUN is important for evoked release and for cooperation between the C1 and C2B domains in membrane binding during repetitive stimulation to generate an activated state that is stabilized by binding of the C1 domain to DAG and of the C2B domain to Ca2+-PIP2.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the structural and functional data.

claim: Reconstitutions including DAG and PIP2 in the T-liposomes may recapitulate more closely an activated state than the normal state that leads to release evoked by a single action potential.
source: Thus, as we noted previously (Liu et al., 2016), our reconstitutions including DAG and PIP2 in the T-liposomes may recapitulate more closely this activated state than the normal state that leads to release evoked by a single action potential.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the reconstitution data.

claim: The crystal structure of Munc13-1 C1C2BMUN and the functional data represent critical steps to understanding how Munc13-1 bridges the vesicle and plasma membranes to control SNARE complex formation.
source: The crystal structure of Munc13–1 C1C2BMUN and the functional data presented here represent critical steps to meet this challenge, revealing a highly elongated structure that is key to understanding how Munc13–1 bridges the vesicle and plasma membranes to control SNARE complex formation, and how the C1 and C2B domains mediate presynaptic plasticity processes that depend on Ca2+ and DAG.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the significance of the work.

claim: The length of C1C2BMUN is close to 20 nm, which is comparable to the radius of a synaptic vesicle.
source: Notable features of the structure of C1C2BMUN include its length, which is close to 20 nm and is thus comparable to the radius of a synaptic vesicle, and the interfaces between its different domains.
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the crystal structure and comparison to known dimensions.

claim: The three mutations designed to disrupt domain interfaces have distinct effects on evoked release, vesicle priming, vesicle release probability, high-frequency stimulation and PDBu-induced facilitation.
source: The observation that the three mutations designed to disrupt domain interfaces observed in the structure have distinct effects on evoked release, vesicle priming, vesicle release probability, high-frequency stimulation and PDBu-induced facilitation demonstrates the functional relevance of the overall structure and shows that the different domain interfaces perturbed by the mutations play differential roles in release and short-term presynaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the functional data.

claim: Each of the three mutations uniquely alters the normal relation between vesicle release probability and steady-state EPSC amplitude in 10 Hz AP trains.
source: This conclusion is further supported by the observation that each of the three mutations uniquely alters the normal relation between vesicle release probability and steady-state EPSC amplitude in 10 Hz AP trains in neurons expressing WT Munc13–1 (Figure 5B), a relation that arises from the natural increase in RRP depletion rate as vesicle release probability increases.
evidence: This is directly observed in the electrophysiological data.

claim: The three mutations change the normal inverse relation between the extent of PDBu-induced facilitation and the vesicle release probability.
source: Similarly, the three mutations also change the normal inverse relation between the extent of PDBu-induced facilitation and the vesicle release probability.
evidence: This is directly observed in the electrophysiological data.

claim: Phorbol ester activation of the Munc13 C1 domain is believed to mimic the effects of increased DAG levels during repetitive stimulation.
source: This finding is not surprising, as the effects of PDBu are likely to be at least partially related to those observed in 10 Hz trains. Thus, phorbol ester activation of the Munc13 C1 domain is believed to mimic the effects of increased DAG levels during repetitive stimulation, which result from accumulation of intracellular Ca2+ and activation of PLCs (Rhee et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Increased DAG levels during repetitive stimulation result from accumulation of intracellular Ca2+ and activation of PLCs.
source: This finding is not surprising, as the effects of PDBu are likely to be at least partially related to those observed in 10 Hz trains. Thus, phorbol ester activation of the Munc13 C1 domain is believed to mimic the effects of increased DAG levels during repetitive stimulation, which result from accumulation of intracellular Ca2+ and activation of PLCs (Rhee et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The C1C2BMUN structure does not support models whereby the C1 and C2B domains impair the activity of the MUN domain by direct intramolecular interactions.
source: Because the C1 and C2B domains pack at the N-terminal end of the long helical structure, far from the middle region of the MUN domain that contains the NF residues involved in opening syntaxin-1 (Yang et al., 2015) (Figure 1B), our structure does not support models whereby the C1 and C2B domains impair the activity of the MUN domain by direct intramolecular interactions, and binding to DAG or Ca2+ releases these inhibitory interactions [e.g. (Rizo and Rosenmund, 2008)].
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial arrangement in the crystal structure.

claim: Activation of Munc13-1 by PDBu or by repetitive stimulation involves cooperative binding of the C1 and C2B domains to the plasma membrane in a defined orientation promoted by increases in DAG and intracellular Ca2+.
source: Instead, our structure suggests that activation of Munc13–1 by PDBu or by repetitive stimulation involves cooperative binding of the C1 and C2B domains to the plasma membrane in a defined orientation that is promoted by increases in the levels of DAG and intracellular Ca2+; this activated state may be more effective in mediating priming and/or downstream events leading to fusion than the state existing under resting conditions, which may involve a different orientation of Munc13–1 with respect to the plasma membrane favored by Ca2+- and DAG-independent interactions involving multiple basic residues of the C1 and C2B domains (Figure 2C; see also Figure 9 and discussion below).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the structural and functional data.

claim: The activated state of Munc13-1 may be more effective in mediating priming and/or downstream events leading to fusion than the resting state.
source: Instead, our structure suggests that activation of Munc13–1 by PDBu or by repetitive stimulation involves cooperative binding of the C1 and C2B domains to the plasma membrane in a defined orientation that is promoted by increases in the levels of DAG and intracellular Ca2+; this activated state may be more effective in mediating priming and/or downstream events leading to fusion than the state existing under resting conditions, which may involve a different orientation of Munc13–1 with respect to the plasma membrane favored by Ca2+- and DAG-independent interactions involving multiple basic residues of the C1 and C2B domains (Figure 2C; see also Figure 9 and discussion below).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the structural and functional data.

claim: The resting state of Munc13-1 may involve a different orientation with respect to the plasma membrane favored by Ca2+- and DAG-independent interactions involving multiple basic residues of the C1 and C2B domains.
source: Instead, our structure suggests that activation of Munc13–1 by PDBu or by repetitive stimulation involves cooperative binding of the C1 and C2B domains to the plasma membrane in a defined orientation that is promoted by increases in the levels of DAG and intracellular Ca2+; this activated state may be more effective in mediating priming and/or downstream events leading to fusion than the state existing under resting conditions, which may involve a different orientation of Munc13–1 with respect to the plasma membrane favored by Ca2+- and DAG-independent interactions involving multiple basic residues of the C1 and C2B domains (Figure 2C; see also Figure 9 and discussion below).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the structural observations.

claim: The V549E,L554E mutation resembles the H567K mutation that is expected to unfold the C1 domain.
source: Overall, the effects of this mutation resemble those caused by the H567K mutation that is expected to unfold the C1 domain (Rhee et al., 2002; Basu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison based on functional similarities and cited literature.

claim: The decreases in RRP observed for both the V549E,L554E and H567K mutants may result from disruption of coupling between the C-terminal region and the N-terminus containing the C2A domain.
source: The decreases in the RRP observed for both the V549E,L554E and the H567K mutants may result from disruption of coupling between the C-terminal region and the N-terminus containing the C2A domain, which contributes to the docking-priming activity of Munc13–1 (MC and CR, unpublished results).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on functional similarities and unpublished data.

claim: The increased release probability observed for both the V549E,L554E and H567K mutants suggests that the disruptive structural effects may mimic to some extent the changes involved in activating Munc13-1 during repetitive stimulation.
source: The increased release probability observed for both mutants suggests that the disruptive structural effects of the two mutations may mimic to some extent the changes involved in activating Munc13–1 during repetitive stimulation, which may involve in part the release of inhibitory effects caused by N-terminal sequences.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on functional data.

claim: The V549E,L554E mutation prevented the increase in Pvr observed after repetitive stimulation for WT Munc13-1.
source: However, note that the V549E,L554E mutation prevented the increase in Pvr observed after repetitive stimulation for WT Munc13–1 (Figure 7E), indicating that different features govern this increase in Pvr and the release probability in naïve synapses.
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The packing of the C2B-MUN interface observed in the C1C2BMUN structure is important for normal vesicle priming and release caused by a single action potential.
source: These results suggest that the packing of the C2B-MUN interface observed in our structure is important for normal vesicle priming and release caused by a single action potential, but the alteration of this interface caused by the N940W mutation favors the activated state that is generated during repetitive stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional effects of the N940W mutation.

claim: The alteration of the C2B-MUN interface caused by the N940W mutation favors the activated state that is generated during repetitive stimulation.
source: These results suggest that the packing of the C2B-MUN interface observed in our structure is important for normal vesicle priming and release caused by a single action potential, but the alteration of this interface caused by the N940W mutation favors the activated state that is generated during repetitive stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional effects of the N940W mutation.

claim: The N940W mutation causes a larger increase in release probability after repetitive stimulation than that observed with WT Munc13-1.
source: This view is reinforced by the finding that the N940W mutation causes a larger increase in release probability after repetitive stimulation than that observed with WT Munc13–1 (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is directly measured in electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The neurotransmitter release machinery is highly complex, including several large proteins that form the active zone in addition to SNAREs, Munc18-1, Munc13-1, NSF, αSNAP, synaptotagmin-1 and multiple additional components.
source: The neurotransmitter release machinery is highly complex, including several large proteins of hundreds of kDa that form the active zone in addition to the SNARES, Munc18–1, Munc13–1, NSF, αSNAP, synaptotagmin-1 and multiple additional components (Südhof, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Without knowing how Munc13-1 interacts with other proteins, interpretation of the C1C2BMUN structure in terms of specific models of neurotransmitter release is necessarily speculative.
source: Without knowing how Munc13–1 interacts with other proteins, interpretation of the structure of Munc13–1 C1C2BMUN in terms of specific models of neurotransmitter release is necessarily speculative.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current data.

claim: The C1C2BMUN structure poses critical constraints on working models of release and its regulation.
source: Nevertheless, the structure poses critical constraints on working models of release and its regulation.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the significance of the structural data.

claim: The Munc13-1 C1C2BMUNC2C fragment bridges V-liposomes to T-liposomes in the absence of Ca2+.
source: For instance, the model of Figure 9A is based on the finding that the Munc13–1 C1C2BMUNC2C fragment bridges V-liposomes to T-liposomes in the absence of Ca2+ (Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous reconstitution study.

claim: Bridging of membranes by Munc13-1 might facilitate the activity of the MUN domain in opening syntaxin-1 to initiate SNARE complex formation.
source: Such bridging might facilitate the activity of the MUN domain in opening syntaxin-1 to initiate SNARE complex formation and may involve interactions of the polybasic face of the C1-C2B region (Figure 2C) with the T-liposomes and of C2C with the V-liposomes.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the structural and functional data.

claim: If Munc13-1 is located between the two membranes, progress toward complete SNARE complex assembly and fusion would require release of Munc13-1 from the fusion complex.
source: Importantly, if Munc13–1 is located between the two membranes, progress toward complete SNARE complex assembly and fusion would require release of Munc13–1 from the fusion complex because otherwise its large size would hinder further membrane proximity.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the size of Munc13-1 and membrane proximity requirements.

claim: In a model where Munc13-1 is released from the fusion complex, Munc13-1 could not underlie changes in release probability directly.
source: In this scenario, Munc13–1 could not underlie changes in release probability directly, but its enhanced activity could lead to an increase in the number of preassembled SNARE complexes that might underlie the increases in release probability caused by up-regulation of DAG, by PDBu treatment or by the K630W mutation in a Ca2+ binding loop of the Munc13–2 C2B domain (Rhee et al., 2002; Shin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of how Munc13-1 might function in this model.

claim: It is difficult to explain with a model where Munc13-1 is released why the H567K mutation does not alter the vesicle refilling rate under resting conditions while increasing the Pvr.
source: However, it is difficult to explain with this type of model why the H567K mutation in the C1 domain does not alter the vesicle refilling rate under resting conditions while increasing the Pvr (Rhee et al., 2002), and why PDBu changes the vesicle release probability without altering the RRP (Basu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a critique of the model based on cited functional data.

claim: The distinct effects of Munc13 mutations on evoked release, RRP, vesicular release probability, synaptic responses to repetitive stimulation and PDBu-dependent facilitation are more readily explained by models postulating that Munc13-1 remains bound to the SNARE complex after SNARE complex assembly.
source: The distinct effects of Munc13 mutations on evoked release, RRP, vesicular release probability, synaptic responses to repetitive stimulation and PDBu-dependent facilitation [Figures 3–7 and (Rhee et al., 2002; Basu et al., 2007; Shin et al., 2010) are more readily explained by models postulating that Munc13–1 remains bound to the SNARE complex and/or other components of the release apparatus after SNARE complex assembly, forming part of the fusion complex.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the functional data.

claim: Models where Munc13-1 remains bound predict at least two major actions for Munc13s: one in docking-priming and another in fusion.
source: Such models predict at least two major actions for Munc13s, one in docking-priming (i.e. orchestrating SNARE complex assembly) and another in fusion.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the functional data.

claim: The length of the C1C2BMUN structure suggests that the Munc13-1 C-terminal region cannot remain in the central space between two membranes after the SNARE complex is even partially assembled.
source: The length of the C1C2BMUN structure suggests that the Munc13–1 C-terminal region cannot remain in the central space between two membranes (as in Figure 9A) after the SNARE complex is even partially assembled.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural dimensions and SNARE complex assembly.

claim: The activities of Munc13-1 in bridging membranes and mediating SNARE complex assembly could be performed with Munc13-1 located in the periphery of the membrane-membrane interface.
source: However, the activities of Munc13–1 in bridging the two membranes and mediating SNARE complex assembly, as well as potential downstream functions, could be performed with Munc13–1 located in the periphery of the membrane-membrane interface, with an arrangement where the large size of Munc13–1 does not hinder completion of SNARE complex assembly and membrane fusion (e.g. Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the structural constraints.

claim: With Munc13-1 at the periphery, reorientation upon binding to DAG and Ca2+-PIP2 could lead to an optimization of the primed state that can lead more readily to membrane fusion upon Ca2+ influx.
source: With such an arrangement, reorientation of Munc13–1 upon binding to DAG and Ca2+-PIP2 could still underlie an increased activity in facilitating SNARE complex formation, but such reorientation could also lead to an optimization of the primed state that can lead more readily to membrane fusion upon Ca2+ influx than that observed without Munc13–1 activation.
evidence: This is a speculative model based on the structural and functional data.

claim: Separation of the roles of Munc13-1 into at least two steps can easily explain the differential effects of the V549E,L554E, R750E,K752E and N940W mutations.
source: This separation of the roles of Munc13–1 into at least two steps can easily explain the differential effects of the V549E,L554E, R750E,K752E and N940W mutations in the different functional assays, including the finding that N940W impairs priming and evoked release, but enhances Munc13–1 function during 10 Hz trains or PDBu treatment (Figures 4–7).
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional data and the proposed model.

claim: The primed fusion complex might contain additional components such as Munc18-1, αSNAP, NSF, synaptotagmin-1 and complexins.
source: Clearly, the primed fusion complex depicted in Figure 9B (top) might contain additional components such as Munc18–1, αSNAP, NSF, synaptotagmin-1 and complexins, among others.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the composition of the fusion complex.

claim: A model with SNAREs on the periphery is consistent with electron microscopy images of SNARE-mediated liposome fusion intermediates.
source: An attractive feature of this model is that it places the SNAREs on the periphery of the membrane-membrane interface rather than between the membranes, consistent with electron microscopy images of SNARE-mediated liposome fusion intermediates (Hernandez et al., 2012) and of presynaptic terminals showing practically direct contact between docked-primed vesicles and the plasma membrane [e.g. (Harlow et al., 2001)].
evidence: This is supported by citations to electron microscopy studies.

claim: Electron microscopy images of presynaptic terminals show practically direct contact between docked-primed vesicles and the plasma membrane.
source: An attractive feature of this model is that it places the SNAREs on the periphery of the membrane-membrane interface rather than between the membranes, consistent with electron microscopy images of SNARE-mediated liposome fusion intermediates (Hernandez et al., 2012) and of presynaptic terminals showing practically direct contact between docked-primed vesicles and the plasma membrane [e.g. (Harlow et al., 2001)].
evidence: This is supported by citation to electron microscopy studies.

claim: With SNAREs on the periphery, the SNARE complex could not induce fusion by bringing the membranes into proximity, but could pull the membranes radially outwards as assembly is completed.
source: With this architecture, the SNARE complex could not induce fusion by bringing the vesicle and plasma membranes into proximity, as they are already in contact before Ca2+ influx, but could pull the two membranes radially outwards as assembly of the SNARE complex is completed (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is a speculative model for the mechanism of SNARE-mediated fusion.

claim: In the proposed model, fusion would result from the tension created in both membranes by SNARE complex assembly.
source: In this case, fusion would result from the tension created in both membranes, which would favor transient formation of non-bilayer intermediates that might or might not resemble a stalk.
evidence: This is a speculative model for the mechanism of membrane fusion.

claim: Components of the fusion complex that bridge the membranes would play an important role to establish support points from which the SNAREs can exert their force on the membranes more efficiently.
source: Components of the fusion complex that are bound to the SNARE complex and bridge the membranes (e.g. Munc13–1 in Figure 9B) would play an important role to establish support points from which the SNAREs can exert their force on the membranes more efficiently.
evidence: This is a speculative model for the role of Munc13-1 in the fusion mechanism.

claim: The strong effect of the R750E,K752E mutation in fusion assays suggests that the reconstitutions recapitulate better the mechanism of release during repetitive stimulation than release evoked by a single action potential.
source: As discussed in the results section, the strong effect of the R750E,K752E mutation in our fusion assays (Figure 8) suggests that our reconstitutions recapitulate better the mechanism of release during repetitive stimulation than release evoked by a single action potential.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of reconstitution and electrophysiology data.

claim: The tight Ca2+ dependence of membrane fusion in reconstitution assays arises largely from Ca2+ binding to the Munc13-1 C2B domain.
source: This proposal is supported by the findings that the tight Ca2+ dependence of membrane fusion in our reconstitution assays (Figure 8) arises largely from Ca2+ binding to the Munc13–1 C2B domain (Liu et al., 2016), and that disrupting the Ca2+-binding sites of the Munc13–2 C2B domain did not impair evoked release in rescue experiments but did impair release during repetitive stimulation (Shin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.
